To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) human tumors growing in patients are coated with a blocking factor that is capable of preventing the killing of tumor cells by lymphocytes immune to the patients' tumor antigens; (b) this blocking factor can be eluted from the tumor cells with pH 3.0 buffer; and (c) the eluted factor consists of at least two components, a high and a low molecular weight one, both of which are necessary for the blocking effect to occur.

human tumor cells, growing in vivo, are coated by “tumor‐specific blocking factors” which can be eluted from the cells at acidic pH, and that these factors are composed of two fractions of different molecular weight, which act synergistically to block lymphocyte‐cytotoxicity.

(i) sera of patients with growing neoplasm contain blocking activity that abrogates tumor‐cell destruction mediated by immune lymphocytes, and that (ii) the blocking activity can be recovered from the tumors by elution at low pH.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the nature of the “blocking factors” and the elucidation of the mechanisms of their production and action.
the study of the mechanisms of tumor escape from the immune system and with the development of new immunotherapeutic strategies.
the study of the mechanisms of tumor immunity and the development of immunotherapeutic approaches for the management of cancer.
